heroIntro: Losing an original registered land title deed (Saf Kabala, Heba, Partition, or Exchange deed) is an alarming experience for property owners in Bangladesh. Whether the deed was misplaced during relocation, damaged by environmental elements, or deliberately withheld by disputing relatives, property owners worry that they have lost their legal title. Under Bangladeshi property jurisprudence, ownership resides in the underlying lawful registration and record of rights, not solely in the physical document. The Registration Act 1908 provides a well-defined statutory procedure to inspect official archives, search volume books (Balam Boi), and procure an authentic certified copy (Nokol) possessing full evidentiary validity in all courts and government land offices.

quickAnswer.title: How Do You Replace a Lost Land Title Deed in Bangladesh?
quickAnswer.text: When an original land deed is lost in Bangladesh, you must immediately file a General Diary (GD) at the local police station and publish a lost document announcement in a recognized daily newspaper. Next, locate the registered deed number, registration year, and relevant Sub-Registry Office. If these details are unknown, apply for an official record search in the Sub-Registry Balam Boi (Volume Books) using Index I or Index II under Section 57 of the Registration Act 1908. Once the volume and page are identified, submit Form No. 36 along with statutory inspection and non-judicial stamp fees to obtain a certified copy (Nokol), which serves as valid secondary evidence under Section 65 of the Evidence Act 1872.
highlights: Filing a Police GD and national newspaper notice protects against fraudulent third-party misuse.
The Sub-Registry Office maintains permanent master records in bound Balam Boi archives.
A certified copy (Nokol) has full statutory evidentiary weight under Section 57 of the Registration Act 1908.
Certified deeds can be utilized for AC Land mutation, bank mortgages, and civil title suits.
points: Governing Statutes: The Registration Act 1908 (Sections 57 & 78) and The Evidence Act 1872 (Section 65).
Key Registry Records: Book No. 1 (Register of non-testamentary documents), Index I (names), and Index II (property).
Statutory Fees: Application fee, search inspection fee per year, non-judicial stamp duty, and copying fee.

sections.title: 1. Immediate Protective Steps: Police GD and Newspaper Notice
sections.content:
The moment you realize an original registered deed is missing, stolen, or misplaced, your immediate priority is to create an official evidentiary record of the loss. This prevents dishonest third parties or fraudulent family members from attempting to create unauthorized mortgage liens or sham powers of attorney using your physical document.

The first mandatory step is filing a General Diary (GD) with the police station (thana) having territorial jurisdiction over the location where the document was misplaced. The GD must state the precise details of the registered deed—including the deed number, date of execution, name of the Sub-Registry Office, mouza, khatian, plot (dag) numbers, and the registered owner's full particulars. If you require guidance on lodging police station records, examine our practical guide on how to file a GD at a Bangladesh police station.

Following the GD, property owners should publish a brief loss announcement in a widely circulated national Bengali or English daily newspaper. The published notice serves as public notice to financial institutions and prospective purchasers that the original deed is missing and that any transaction conducted on the basis of the missing physical document is unauthorized and subject to legal challenge.

sections.title: 2. The Archive System: Understanding Balam Boi and Registry Indexes
sections.content:
Many landowners assume that if the paper deed in their custody is gone, proof of ownership disappears. In reality, Bangladesh maintains a centralized, permanent archival recording system under the Registration Act 1908. Every Sub-Registry Office maintains physical and increasingly digitized record books known as Balam Boi (Volume Books).

When a deed is registered, the Sub-Registry Office copies the entire text and hand-drawn property sketch verbatim into Book No. 1 ('Register of non-testamentary documents relating to immovable property'). The volume is bound into permanent books and assigned a specific Volume (Balam) number, Book number, and Page numbers. These historical volumes are permanently preserved in the district record rooms (Record Mahal) under the authority of the District Registrar.

To enable public retrieval, the registry office maintains statutory cross-reference indexes pursuant to Section 54 of the Registration Act 1908. Index I records the names of all executing parties and claimants in alphabetical order. Index II records the property particulars arranged by Mouza, sheet, and plot numbers. These indexes allow records to be traced even when original paperwork has been lost for decades.

sections.title: 3. How to Search When Deed Number or Year Is Unknown
sections.content:
A frequent challenge arises when property was purchased decades ago by parents or grandparents, and the heirs know the plot location but have no record of the deed number or exact registration year. In this scenario, obtaining a certified copy requires an official archive search (Talashi).

Under Section 57(1) of the Registration Act 1908, any person may inspect Book No. 1 and its related indexes upon payment of the statutory inspection fees. To initiate an index search, you must submit an application identifying the relevant Sub-Registry Office (such as Tejgaon, Uttara, Dhanmondi, or a specific Upazila registry), the Mouza name, and the approximate year or multi-year range of the transaction.

The registry searcher reviews Index II for the specified Mouza and plot number across the designated years. When a matching entry is discovered, the index discloses the exact registered deed number, volume number, and page range. Once these reference numbers are established, the path is clear to apply for the certified copy.

sections.title: 4. Step-by-Step Procedure to Apply for a Certified Copy (Nokol)
sections.content:
Once the deed number, volume number, and year of registration are identified, obtaining the official certified copy (Nokol) proceeds through a structured statutory workflow:

  1. Submission of Form No. 36: Procure and complete the prescribed statutory application form (Form No. 36) addressed to the Sub-Registrar. Detail the deed number, year, volume, page number, donor/donee names, and property description.
  2. Affixing Court Fees: Affix the required Court Fee stamp to the application header as mandated by the Court Fees Act 1870.
  3. Payment of Search and Inspection Fees: Pay the statutory search fees covering the relevant archive years under Section 78 of the Registration Act 1908.
  4. Payment of Copying Stamp Fees: Deposit the requisite non-judicial stamps and copying fees. Currently, certified copies require non-judicial stamps under Article 24 of Schedule I of the Stamp Act 1899, plus fixed government folios (cartridge paper fees).
  5. Transcription and Comparison: The Sub-Registry copying section (Nokol Nobish) transcribes the deed from the master Balam Boi onto official stamped folios. A comparison officer (Taqabila) reads and verifies the transcript against the original book record.
  6. Certification and Seal: The Sub-Registrar applies the official embossed seal, certifies the document as a true copy of the record under Section 57(5) of the Registration Act 1908, signs the certification, and issues the document to the applicant.

sections.title: 5. Government Fee Schedule for Inspections and Certified Copies
sections.content:
All fees for searching archives and procuring certified copies of registered deeds are determined by government statutory regulatory orders (SROs) promulgated under Section 78 of the Registration Act 1908 and the Stamp Act 1899. The following fee ranges reflect official government schedules as verified for the 2026 operational year:

  • Application Court Fee: Nominal court fee stamp (typically 20 to 50 BDT) affixed to the initial application.
  • Search Fee (Deed Number Known): Searching records for a single specified year incurs an official fee of approximately 50 BDT.
  • Multi-Year Index Search Fee (Deed Number Unknown): When a multi-year search across Index I or II is required, the statutory fee is charged per year searched (typically 50 to 100 BDT per year).
  • Non-Judicial Stamp for Certified Copy: Non-judicial stamp duty under the Stamp Act 1899 (currently 50 BDT for non-testamentary instruments) must be deposited.
  • Folio / Transcription Fees: A per-page transcription fee (calculated per 300 words or per cartridge folio, roughly 100 to 200 BDT per folio) covers copying and comparison.
  • Urgent Processing Surcharge: An optional expedited processing fee can be deposited for urgent deliveries within 3 to 7 working days.

Always ensure that official government receipts (Dakhila) are collected for all fees deposited at the registry treasury counter. Confirm current fee schedules with your advocate before filing.

sections.title: 6. Summary Matrix: Document Types, Search Protocols & Timeline
sections.content:
Different types of missing real estate records require slightly different search workflows. The following matrix outlines the procedural roadmap across common property deed categories in Bangladesh:

sections.title: 7. Evidentiary Value of a Certified Copy in Civil Court and AC Land Mutation
sections.content:
A widespread concern among landowners who hold a certified copy instead of the original deed is whether the copy carries identical legal validity. The statutory framework provides complete reassurance on this point.

Under Section 57(5) of the Registration Act 1908, a certified copy given under the official hand and seal of the registering officer 'shall be admissible for the purpose of proving the contents of the original document.' In civil litigation, while Section 64 of the Evidence Act 1872 establishes that documents must generally be proved by primary evidence (the original document itself), Section 65(f) expressly permits secondary evidence when the document is a public record within the meaning of Section 74, or when it is a certified copy permitted by the Registration Act.

Similarly, the Ministry of Land and the Assistant Commissioner (Land) offices across Bangladesh routinely accept certified Nokols for the purposes of mutation (Namjari), creation of new Khatians, and payment of land development taxes (Khajna). A certified copy, accompanied by the police GD number confirming loss of the primary document, is fully recognized by commercial banks for title verification and property conveyancing. sections.title: 8. Illustrative Scenario: Tracing a 30-Year-Old Missing Saf Kabala
sections.content:
To demonstrate how an archive search and Nokol procurement unfold in practice, consider the following illustrative scenario (composite; names and details changed).

An expatriate living in Sydney inherited two plots of prime residential land in Uttara, Dhaka, originally purchased by his late father in 1994. While organizing family affairs following the father's death, the family discovered that the physical Saf Kabala deed was missing from the family safe, and no relative possessed a photocopy noting the registration serial number. Without the deed, the AC Land office declined to process the mutation into the heirs' names.

The heir retained an advocate in Dhaka to conduct a comprehensive archival retrieval. The legal team first obtained the original RS and City Jarip Khatians from the Dhaka Collectorate record room to establish the exact Mouza name, CS/SA/RS plot numbers, and the late father's recorded name. Armed with these property coordinates, the advocate submitted an application under Section 57 of the Registration Act 1908 at the relevant Sub-Registry Office for an Index II inspection spanning the years 1992 through 1996.

Within ten days, the registry searchers located the entry in the 1994 Index II, revealing Deed No. 4582 recorded in Volume 48, pages 112 through 126 of Book No. 1. The advocate deposited the required statutory cartridge paper fees and non-judicial stamps. Within one week, the Sub-Registrar issued an official certified Nokol bearing the embossed government seal. Using this certified document and a succession certificate, the heirs successfully mutated the land records into their names without dispute.

sections.title: 9. Remote Deed Procurement Protocols for Non-Resident Bangladeshis
sections.content:
Non-resident Bangladeshis residing in the United States, United Kingdom, Canada, Australia, and the Middle East face unique logistical barriers when deeds are misplaced in Bangladesh. Traveling to Bangladesh merely to attend registry counters is both expensive and unnecessary.

To safely procure a certified copy of a missing land deed from abroad without international travel, follow these established legal steps:

  • Gather Baseline Land Identifiers: Review existing Khatians (CS, SA, RS, BS), land tax receipts (dakhila), or municipal tax bills to note the Mouza, Upazila/Thana, and plot numbers.
  • Engage a Licensed Advocate via Remote Consultation: Retain an advocate practicing in the relevant district to represent your interests before the Sub-Registry Office.
  • File an Online Police GD: In many metropolitan jurisdictions including Dhaka Metropolitan Police (DMP), a General Diary for lost property can be filed through the official DMP Online GD portal, providing immediate digital GD verification.
  • Authorize Record Searches: Instruct your advocate to conduct the Balam Boi search under Section 57 of the Registration Act 1908.
  • Secure Attested Courier Dispatch: Once certified by the Sub-Registrar, the advocate can have the certified document apostilled or attested by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA) in Dhaka if required for foreign embassy submissions, and securely dispatched to your overseas address via tracked international courier.

For additional assistance with remote property management, review our specialized services for land dispute resolution and NRB legal services in Bangladesh.

faqs.question: If I lose my original land deed, do I lose ownership of my property in Bangladesh?
faqs.answer: No. Ownership is established by the legal registration of the document in the government registry and the recorded title in the Khatians, not solely by physical possession of the original paper. A certified copy issued by the Sub-Registry Office legally proves your ownership.

faqs.question: What is a Nokol (নকল) in Bangladeshi property law?
faqs.answer: A Nokol is an official certified copy of a registered deed transcribed directly from the master volume book (Balam Boi) and certified under the seal and signature of the Sub-Registrar pursuant to Section 57 of the Registration Act 1908.

faqs.question: Can someone fraudulently sell my land if they possess my lost original deed?
faqs.answer: It is illegal to sell property without valid title. However, dishonest individuals may attempt fraud or take private loans. Filing an immediate police GD and publishing a newspaper notice legally invalidates unauthorized transactions based on the missing deed.

faqs.question: How can I find my lost deed if I do not know the deed number or year of registration?
faqs.answer: You can apply for an archival search under Section 57 of the Registration Act 1908. The Sub-Registry Office will search Index I (by parties' names) or Index II (by Mouza and plot numbers) across the estimated years to identify the deed number and volume.

faqs.question: Is a certified copy accepted by banks for mortgage loan applications in Bangladesh?
faqs.answer: Yes. Most commercial banks accept a certified Nokol accompanied by the police GD, newspaper publication, and complete chain of title records, subject to verification against the Sub-Registry Balam Boi by the bank's panel lawyer.

faqs.question: Can I mutate (Namjari) my land using a certified copy of a lost deed?
faqs.answer: Yes. Assistant Commissioner (Land) offices across Bangladesh routinely accept certified copies of registered deeds for mutation applications, provided the document is certified by the Sub-Registrar and verified in the registry records.

faqs.question: How long does it take to obtain a certified copy of a deed from the Sub-Registry Office?
faqs.answer: If the deed number and year are known, it generally takes 5 to 14 working days. If an archive index search is required across multiple historical years, the process typically takes two to four weeks.

faqs.question: Can an overseas Bangladeshi obtain a certified deed without returning to Bangladesh?
faqs.answer: Yes. An overseas Bangladeshi can authorize an advocate in Bangladesh to conduct the search and retrieve the certified copy under Section 57 of the Registration Act 1908, with documents dispatched abroad via tracked courier.
